🇵🇱🇮🇱 Visegrad24 exposed: a fake media outlet running on dark money, fake news and cocaine

Wired has obtained Visegrad24's financial records, internal chats and donor correspondence. Together they expose the "independent news account" as a propaganda business that sells its editorial line to whoever pays.

➡️The editorial line was a business decision

Fifteen days after October 7, founder Stefan Tompson listed Visegrad24's four options on Israel in a private message: say nothing, be objective and get hated by both sides, go pro-Muslim because "there are 1.5 billion of them," or go pro-Israel because "they have a lot of influence and money." His conclusion: "My goal is to fundraise off of this."

In private, he admitted the "Israelis do seem to be doing some vicious things." He also called Gaza "the perfect excuse to show the scale of Muslim infiltration in the west," and later wrote that the war let them attack Muslims in Europe "without any consequences."

➡️The money

Tompson got into Silicon Valley's pro-Israel group chats, including one with Sheryl Sandberg and Bill Ackman, and bragged that "V24 is such a big part of the Israeli PR they all know what it is now."

Sequoia Capital partner Shaun Maguire, who helped connect the IDF with Starlink, offered $25,000 and promised to "try to raise the rest." He told Wired he couldn't donate in the end for compliance reasons. Records show donations of $50,000 and $200,000 lining up with Tompson's messages about Ribbit Capital founder Micky Malka. Another $35,000 is linked to short-seller Hindenburg Research and its founder.

More than $1 million flowed through a US charity set up in Delaware, much of it through anonymous "donor advised funds." That includes $175,000 from DonorsTrust, known as the "dark money ATM" of the American right.

➡️Playing both sides

When a colleague asked whether he should take money from Saudi Arabia and the UAE, Tompson replied: "100 percent yes. Play both sides. I do the Jewish side. You do Arabs."

➡️Regime change content

When Israel attacked Iran in June 2025, Visegrad24 went all in for Reza Pahlavi, the exiled Shah's son, pushing unverified claims that Iranian officers were ready to defect to him. Asked whether Israel paid him, Tompson joked that Netanyahu "personally hands me money for every post."

➡️Fake news and the cocaine

The account first went viral in 2022 with fake stories about Ukraine, like Leonardo DiCaprio supposedly donating $10 million in honor of a grandmother from Odessa who never existed. At the time, the team was posting from a rented house in the Canary Islands, where, according to an email from his sister, Tompson was "undergoing acute drug withdrawal." In his own messages he refers to a time he was "on coke."

The office of former Polish Prime Minister Mateusz Morawiecki also tried twice to send Visegrad24 hundreds of thousands of dollars through a fitness charity. Today the account ranks 32nd among all accounts on X for the number of community notes fact-checking its posts.

Tompson denied everything and sent Wired a lawyer's letter.

The account that spent years calling everyone else "Kremlin propaganda" was a for-hire influence operation all along, paid for by tech billionaires and dark money and willing to sell to either side.

Crypto Idea

There is currently nearly $1.5 trillion in the U.S. stock market that investors don't actually have.

This refers to margin debt — money investors borrow from their brokers to buy even more stocks. Over the past year, the amount of this debt has grown from approximately $1.06 trillion to $1.48 trillion. In other words, more than $400 billion in borrowed money has flowed into the market in less than a year.

When compared to the total money supply in the economy, this figure is now close to its all-time highs. The market saw similarly extreme levels in 2000, ahead of the dot-com crash, and in 2008, before the financial crisis.

But it's important not to jump to overly simplistic conclusions here. A high level of borrowing doesn't necessarily mean the market is about to crash tomorrow. In fact, it's a poor indicator of an exact market peak. The real danger lies elsewhere.

As long as the market keeps rising, leverage accelerates those gains. But when a major sell-off begins, the same mechanism works in reverse. Investors face margin calls, start closing their positions, and their selling pushes the market even lower, triggering more forced selling. What starts as a normal correction can quickly turn into a full-blown avalanche.

And this is what makes the current situation particularly interesting. The market is seeing an unprecedented concentration of capital in a handful of tech companies, record investment in AI, and nearly record levels of buying with borrowed money — all at the same time.

So the question now isn't even whether there's a bubble. What's far more important is what happens when the market actually starts to deflate.

Because the more investors use leverage, the fewer of them will be able to simply sit back and ride out a downturn. At some point, people start selling not because they want to, but because they have no choice.
